extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of law, comparative legal institutions, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes evaluative criteria and standards the chapter uses to assess the legal profession (the Bar) and the judiciary (the Bench) in comparative perspective, including ethical, institutional, and procedural dimensions. Useful for evaluating quality, integrity, and organization of legal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social standing: wealth and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth and education are the principal elements on which social standing depends in a democratic country; the Bar ranks high in education though not always in wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: leading lawyers may have large incomes in a few great cities, but generally lawyers do not amass the fortunes of industrialists; most lawyers have college training and form part of the intellectual elite of towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and public responsibilities of the legal profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are confidential advisers and depositaries of clients' secrets and can promote or restrain vexatious litigation, become accomplices in chicane, or check abuse of legal rights where morality requires restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should consider whether the profession helps to maintain community tone and commercial morality, and whether lawyers exercise influence on the magistracy responsibly (e.g., by shaming unjust judges rather than misusing influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics and maintenance of tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bar should maintain its own tone and thereby help maintain the tone of the community; codes of legal ethics and etiquette are instruments to secure professional virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for evidence of decadence (e.g., lawyers seduced by corporate wealth), and consider the effectiveness of bar associations' efforts to establish and enforce codes of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the profession: separation vs fusion (barristers/attorneys)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether barristers and solicitors (advocates and attorneys) are separate or united affects the profession, the client, and the community; there are distinct arguments from each viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should weigh: profession's interests (opportunities and specialisation), client's interests (continuity and speed of service), and community interest (maintenance of high professional tone and discipline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of representation (single practitioner handling whole case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients generally prefer one person to handle a case from start to finish; keeping a case in one office often reduces mistakes and oversights because the advocate knows the facts and witnesses better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether divided roles (preparer vs advocate) produce coordination failures or whether unity of representation improves efficiency and accuracy of case handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency / despatch of business
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems in which a small number of leading counsel and judges are in constant contact (English plan) tend to be more conducive to the prompt despatch of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how institutional familiarity between judges and counsel affects case speed, knowledge of when 'enough' has been said, and overall expedition of court business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional discipline and cultivable esprit de corps
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easier to maintain a high tone and strict control in a small, specialized body than in a large, mixed body where many members are practically businessmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the occupational structure fosters a warm professional feeling and effective peer regulation or instead diffuses standards among many who see themselves as businesspeople.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict risks when advocate is also attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same person prepares the case and advocates it in court, there is greater temptation to win by doubtful means (e.g., leading witnesses, speculating in client's shares, taking payment as share of proceeds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider conflict-of-interest risks and whether institutional separations/checks reduce unconscious or deliberate abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: External symbols of judicial dignity and their functional effect
rubrics_metrics.description: External badges of dignity (robes, attendants, ceremonial escort) raise a judge's sense of position and responsibility and affect public respect; their absence can lower perceived dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the presence or absence of formal trappings influences judicial self-regard, public deference, and ultimately the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, tenure, and remuneration of judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Small salaries, limited tenure (often short terms), and methods of appointment (e.g., popular election, party influence) deter the ablest lawyers and can lower the Bench's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how appointment methods, term length, and pay influence who seeks and accepts judicial office and whether they produce independence or subservience to political interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications, learning and capacity of judges (Federal vs State)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of judges varies widely: Federal Supreme Court judges retain dignity and high quality; many State judges in some States are of more limited attainment and sometimes inferior to practising counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare jurisdictions: look for which courts attract prosperous barristers or professors and which do not; consider impact on legal reasoning and adjudication quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific accuracy and certainty of judicial opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some State courts opinions lack scientific accuracy and make the law loose and uncertain; strong courts (Federal, best States, English precedent) mitigate this problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate judicial opinions for doctrinal precision, clarity, and contribution to stable, predictable law; note whether appellate/Federal decisions supply needed authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of criminal justice: speed, technicality, and leniency
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal justice is criticized as slow, overtechnical, uncertain, and unduly lenient; procedural complexity gives opportunities for delay and escape, and weak juries contribute to failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess criminal procedure for excessive technicality, procedural delay, jury performance, and whether stronger judicial control could reduce trivial points and expedite convictions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and integrity of juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Weakness or corruption of juries is blamed for some failings in criminal justice; institutions (e.g., offices like a Warden of the Grand Jury) are sometimes created to safeguard juries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine jury selection, oversight, and local practices for signs of venality or incompetence, and whether institutional safeguards exist and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial corruption and susceptibility to undue influence
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain places suspicions (and some proven cases) exist that judges have been perverted by considerations, bribes, or undue influence; scandalous examples (e.g., Tweed Ring) illustrate extreme corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate incidence of suspected bribery, secret understandings between judges and counsel, appointment of unfit judges to secure political ends, and the mechanisms (elections, short terms) that enable these abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial reforms: codes, education, partnerships, and mobility between branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested improvements include bar associations' codes of ethics and etiquette, easier passage between branches, permitting open partnerships among barristers, and joint education/examination in professional law schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reform proposals, consider practical effects on discipline, mobility, client service, and maintenance of professional standards; these are recommended 'useful minor changes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of concentrated commercial wealth on professional virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of enormously rich and powerful corporations willing to pay vast sums for questionable services has seduced the virtue of some counsel and contributed to decadence in some city Bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which market pressures and high-paying clients distort professional choices, create perverse incentives, and erode ethical norms in particular jurisdictions.
